body:
Why crafts expanded

The Sultanate economy supported many occupations beyond farming. Urban households, nobles, merchants, soldiers and the royal court required cloth, weapons, leather goods, utensils, furniture, buildings and other manufactured articles.

Craft production took place in both towns and villages. Some artisans worked independently or for merchants, while others produced goods for the royal household or powerful nobles.

Textile production and its stages

Cotton textiles were among India's important manufactured products. Turning harvested cotton into cloth required several distinct operations.

  • Ginning: separating seeds from cotton fibres.
  • Carding: cleaning, loosening and arranging the fibres for spinning.
  • Spinning: twisting fibres into yarn.
  • Weaving: interlacing threads to produce fabric.
  • Dyeing and printing: adding colour or patterns, either before or after weaving according to the technique.

Different workers could specialise in different stages. This division of work helped sustain specialised occupations and commercial production.

The spinning wheel or charkha

The charkha, or spinning wheel, became an important technology in medieval textile production. Evidence of its use becomes prominent in sources from the 13th–14th centuries.

The spinning wheel enabled a spinner to rotate a spindle through a wheel-driven mechanism, increasing the speed of yarn production. However, older hand-spindle techniques continued to be used, particularly where their particular qualities were useful.

Increased yarn production could support greater output of cloth, but the amount and quality of fabric also depended on weaving skills, raw materials and market demand.

Other important crafts

Several occupations supplied everyday goods and the needs of the court:

  • Metalworkers produced tools, weapons, armour and utensils.
  • Carpenters and builders made furniture, structures and equipment.
  • Leatherworkers supplied footwear, harnesses and other leather goods.
  • Paper makers and bookbinders supported the growing use of manuscripts, records and correspondence.
  • Stoneworkers and masons participated in construction using arches, domes and improved masonry techniques.

The increased use of paper supported administration and the copying of books. The spread of true arches, domes and suitable mortar expanded building possibilities. These technologies developed through interaction among existing Indian practices, skilled workers and techniques circulating across regions.

Karkhanas: workshops serving the ruler

Karkhanas were royal or elite establishments used for manufacturing, storing or maintaining goods required by the household and administration.

The Sultan's royal karkhanas supplied items such as clothing, furnishings, equipment and articles needed for ceremonial and military purposes. They were not simply ordinary retail shops: their principal function was to meet the requirements of the ruler and his establishment.

Private artisans and merchant-linked workshops, by contrast, could produce goods intended for sale in markets. A skilled worker might therefore serve very different customers depending on where and for whom the work was performed.

Under Firuz Shah Tughluq, enslaved workers were also trained and employed in royal establishments. This illustrates how craft production, royal demand and the institution of slavery could intersect.

Prelims focus

  • Charkha: spinning wheel used in yarn production.
  • Ginning: removal of seeds from cotton.
  • Carding: preparation of cotton fibres for spinning.
  • Karkhanas: royal or elite production and storage establishments.
  • Paper-making, textile production and masonry were important medieval crafts.
  • Trap: A royal karkhana was not necessarily a workshop producing goods for open-market sale.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 6, Towns, Traders and Craftspersons, printed pp. 78–82, 2020–21 edition; IGNOU, eGyanKosh, Economy of the Delhi Sultanate, Unit 22, Technology and Crafts, sections 22.3–22.5, consulted 19 November 2026; IGNOU, eGyanKosh, Indian Polity: The Sultanate, Unit 16, sections on the royal household and administrative establishments, consulted 19 November 2026.]

title: Craft Production, Textile Technology and Royal Workshops

body:
What is urbanisation?

Urbanisation is the development and expansion of towns and cities, where significant numbers of people undertake administrative, military, commercial, craft and service activities in addition to or instead of agriculture.

During the Sultanate period, the growth of states, armies and commercial activity supported important urban centres. Cities consumed agricultural produce, employed artisans and brought together merchants from different regions.

How different types of towns developed

Town typeMain characteristicExample or connection
Administrative capitalResidence of the ruler and government officialsDelhi
Garrison townFortified settlement housing soldiersSiri
Commercial townMarkets, merchants and craft productionDelhi and several regional centres
Port townConnections between inland trade and maritime exchangeKhambat in Gujarat

A town could perform more than 1 function. Delhi was simultaneously an administrative centre, a military centre and an important market city.

How rural production supported cities

Farmers supplied grain and raw materials. Taxes and purchases transferred part of this produce to towns, where it fed soldiers, officials and other residents.

Those residents required clothing, building materials, utensils and services. This created demand for artisans and merchants. In turn, towns provided markets for agricultural surpluses and manufactured goods.

The growth of a city therefore depended partly on its connections with surrounding villages, roads and distant trading centres.

Markets and the movement of goods

Medieval commercial networks included permanent shops, local markets, itinerant traders and organised caravans.

The Banjaras transported substantial quantities of grain using bullocks. Their caravans, called tandas, connected producing areas with towns and military camps.

Other merchants carried valuable commodities such as cloth, horses, spices and metals over long distances. Inns and rest houses along important routes assisted travellers and commercial exchange.

Coinage and monetary exchange

Metal coins facilitated payments to soldiers, purchases in markets and the collection of some taxes. Iltutmish is associated with the establishment of the silver tanka and copper jital as important Sultanate coins.

Moneychangers and merchants helped exchange different currencies and provide commercial services. At the same time, payment in grain and other goods remained important, especially in rural transactions.

Trade beyond the subcontinent

Indian manufactured goods moved through inland routes and maritime networks connecting the subcontinent with West Asia, East Africa, Southeast Asia and China.

Cotton textiles, fine cloth and spices were important goods in these exchanges. Horses were also a significant import because cavalry was central to the military establishment.

Khambat, also known as Cambay, was an important port in Gujarat. Its inland connections and access to maritime routes helped link western Indian production with overseas commerce.

What Ibn Battuta observed about cities

The 14th-century traveller Ibn Battuta described Delhi and Daulatabad as large, populated cities with busy markets. He noted that bazaars were not only places for buying and selling: they could also host social and cultural activities.

He described the demand for Indian textiles in foreign markets and noted that especially fine varieties of muslin were expensive enough to be accessible mainly to wealthy consumers.

His observations illustrate urban prosperity in particular places and periods. They do not imply that every town was equally prosperous or free from disruption caused by war and political instability.

Prelims focus

  • Siri: garrison town associated with Alauddin Khalji.
  • Khambat or Cambay: important medieval port in Gujarat.
  • Silver tanka and copper jital: important coinage associated with Iltutmish.
  • Tanda: caravan of Banjaras.
  • Ibn Battuta: traveller who described the crowded markets and urban life of 14th-century India.
  • Trap: A market town, a port and a garrison town describe functions; a single town could perform several of them.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 6, Towns, Traders and Craftspersons, printed pp. 75–85, and Chapter 7, printed pp. 94–95, 2020–21 edition; NCERT, Themes in Indian History–Part II, Class 12, Chapter 5, Through the Eyes of Travellers, sections 5.2–5.3, printed pp. 127–129; NIOS, Senior Secondary History, Lesson 9, sections on Iltutmish and Sultanate coinage, consulted 19 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: How village production, towns and Gujarat's port trade were connected.

title: Urbanisation, Towns, Markets and Commercial Networks

body:
A socially diverse society

Sultanate society included cultivators, rural chiefs, merchants, artisans, soldiers, religious specialists, government officials, nobles and enslaved people. Their occupations, resources and legal positions varied considerably.

Political authority was concentrated among rulers and influential elites, but the production of food and manufactured goods depended on the work of cultivators and artisans.

Social groups and their roles

GroupPrincipal roleImportant distinction
Nobles and commandersGovernment, military service and provincial authorityPower often depended on royal appointment
Rural chiefs and headmenLocal authority and revenue administrationSome held longstanding local influence
CultivatorsProduction of agricultural goodsMajor source of agrarian revenue
ArtisansProduction of cloth, metal goods and other craftsCould work in villages, towns or royal establishments
Merchants and transportersExchange and movement of goodsConnected regional and long-distance markets
Enslaved peopleVaried forms of service and labourHad an unfree legal and social position

Social mobility: possibilities and restrictions

Social mobility means movement between positions of different social status, wealth or power.

Some people rose to high office through military skill, personal service or royal patronage. The careers of selected trained slaves and other dependants demonstrate that political advancement did not always follow hereditary status.

However, such advancement was exceptional and depended heavily on the ruler's favour. It did not remove the wider inequalities associated with birth, wealth, gender or dependence.

At the level of ordinary occupations, commercial growth could increase opportunities for successful merchants and specialised artisans. Some communities gained wealth or local influence through trade, cultivation or military service.

Varna, jati and changing occupations

Many communities continued to be organised through varna and jati distinctions. A varna referred to a broad social category in Brahmanical classifications, while a jati was a more specific social group commonly associated with birth and customary practices.

As occupations became more specialised, separate artisan and occupational jatis gained recognition. Society was not organised according to a single uniform pattern, however. Tribal and nomadic groups maintained different forms of social organisation, and their interaction with settled communities produced gradual changes.

The Bhils, spread across western and central India, and the Kolis, present in parts of Gujarat and neighbouring regions, provide examples of communities whose livelihoods and relations with settled society differed according to place and period.

Slavery and labour

Slavery was an important institution in the Sultanate period. Enslaved people could be employed in domestic service, the royal household, military establishments, craft production and other forms of work.

Some individuals entered slavery through warfare or trade, while others were acquired through established markets and patronage networks. Their experiences were not uniform.

Elite military slaves and ordinary enslaved workers

The bandagan promoted by rulers such as Iltutmish were selected and trained for important service. Some acquired considerable authority and became commanders or governors.

By contrast, many enslaved workers performed routine or skilled labour without comparable political opportunities. Both categories involved unfree status, but their functions and positions differed greatly.

Under Firuz Shah Tughluq, the administration maintained a department associated with enslaved dependants, known as the Diwan-i-Bandagan. Enslaved artisans could also be employed in royal karkhanas.

Urban growth and social change

The expansion of towns drew merchants, workers, craftsmen and dependants into urban centres. A skilled artisan might find employment through a merchant or a royal establishment. A successful trader might accumulate wealth without becoming a military noble.

Similarly, a trained military slave might acquire political office while remaining tied to a system of personal dependence. Economic success, political authority and personal freedom were different dimensions of social position.

Prelims focus

  • Bandagan: trained military slaves who could hold high office.
  • Diwan-i-Bandagan: department associated with enslaved dependants under Firuz Shah Tughluq.
  • Jati: specific social grouping associated with customary and hereditary practices.
  • Bhils: important communities of western and central India.
  • Kolis: communities present in Gujarat and other western Indian regions.
  • Trap: The rise of selected slaves to high office did not mean that slavery ceased to be a system of unfree labour.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 3, The Delhi Sultans, printed pp. 37–38, and Chapter 7, Tribes, Nomads and Settled Communities, printed pp. 91–97, 2020–21 edition; IGNOU, eGyanKosh, Urbanisation and Urban Centres, Unit 17, section 17.7.2, Institution of Slavery and a New Urban Culture, consulted 19 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Bandagan may rise politically while unfree; artisans can be skilled yet unfree, and merchants wealthy without military nobility.
pictures.caption: Why occupation, wealth, legal status and political power must be distinguished.

title: Sultanate Society: Social Groups, Mobility and Slavery
